tldr: By using the laws of physics—specifically 6D wrenches (forces and torques)—as a shared anchor, tactile data from vastly different sensor types can be unified into a single representation that generalizes across diverse sensors, unseen hardware, and contact-rich robotic manipulation.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed method. Sensor-specific input adapters tokenize diverse tactile signals, which are then aggregated into a 768-dimensional feature vector using a shared Transformer and a physical query. Through 6D wrench reconstruction and embedding alignment with an EMA encoder, the model learns a shared feature space grounded in contact physics.
overview:
For robots to perform delicate assembly and object manipulation, vision alone is not enough—they need a sense of touch to feel forces and torques during contact. In practice, however, tactile sensors rely on completely different working principles and output formats: optical sensors capture elastomer deformation with cameras, magnetic sensors detect magnetic field variations, and piezoresistive sensors measure resistance changes. As a result, tactile data collected on one sensor is notoriously hard to reuse on another, which has stalled the development of large-scale foundation models like those in computer vision.

To tackle this, the authors returned to a first principle: regardless of how a sensor works, any physical contact obeys Newtonian mechanics. Instead of trying to directly align tactile observations across sensors, why not ground all of them into a shared physical quantity: a 6D wrench (3D force and 3D torque)?

To bring this idea to life, the team built a dedicated data acquisition platform pairing 24 different tactile sensors with a force/torque sensor to synchronously record contact motions and 6D wrenches. This yielded a massive dataset of over 100 million tactile-wrench pairs. Using this data, they introduced "TaF-Foundation," a learning framework that combines sensor-specific adapters, a shared Transformer, wrench reconstruction, and embedding alignment.

Evaluations show that the learned representations reduce contact force and torque estimation errors by 14% to 17% over baselines and demonstrate remarkable performance in cross-sensor retrieval (matching the same contact state across different sensors). Furthermore, the representations adapt efficiently to unseen sensors with minimal data and achieve significantly higher success rates in contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks such as key insertion and board wiping.
contributions: Built one of the largest foundation datasets in tactile sensing, capturing over 100 million synchronized tactile–6D wrench pairs across 24 sensors spanning four distinct sensing principles.
Introduced a unified tactile encoder combining sensor-specific adapters with a shared Transformer, grounded in physical contact via wrench reconstruction and EMA-based embedding alignment.

Established an efficient few-shot adaptation protocol for unseen sensors and developed "TaF-Policy" for contact manipulation, achieving substantial performance gains in both simulation and real-world experiments.

sections.heading: Why is tactile data so hard to unify? Breaking the barrier with Newtonian mechanics
sections.summary: Because tactile sensors differ wildly in their sensing principles and formats, sharing data and scaling pre-training has been difficult. This paper overcomes that barrier by using Newtonian mechanics—specifically 6D wrenches—as a shared physical reference for all sensors.
sections.details:
To handle objects dexterously, robots need to understand not only what they see (vision) but also how they physically interact with the environment (touch). Visual camera feeds make it difficult to infer precise contact states, such as how much force is applied or whether an object is about to slip.

However, tactile hardware is extraordinarily diverse. There are optical (vision-based) sensors that record elastomer deformation with cameras, magnetic sensors tracking minute displacements of magnets, and piezoresistive sensors measuring electrical resistance changes. Their output formats range from RGB images to 1D vectors and 2D pressure matrices. This severe heterogeneity makes it very difficult to share or reuse tactile data across sensors, hindering the development of large-scale representation models comparable to those in vision or language.

Prior work has explored self-supervised learning and cross-sensor observation alignment, but collecting direct sensor-to-sensor paired data is tough, limiting both dataset scale and sensor diversity. This motivated the authors' core question: "Can large-scale supervision from directly measured physical quantities (6D wrenches) yield a unified tactile representation that generalizes to unseen hardware?"

The key to their approach is using the 6D wrench (3 translational forces + 3 rotational torques) as a universal reference signal for all sensors. Sensors never need to be paired directly with each other; simply pairing each sensor's observations with wrench measurements is enough to build a shared feature space grounded in contact physics. The authors collected over 100 million pairs to train a unified encoder and built a manipulation policy called TaF-Policy.

sections.heading: Evolution of prior work and the power of directly measured 6D wrenches
sections.summary: Tactile representation learning has evolved from single-sensor self-supervision to cross-sensor alignment, but has lacked large-scale physical grounding. By leveraging directly measured 6D wrenches at scale, this method builds representations truly anchored in contact mechanics.
sections.details:
### The Heterogeneity Challenge in Tactile Sensing
Tactile sensors produce radically different signals depending on their sensing mechanism. Optical sensors output image sequences, while magnetic or resistive sensors output multi-channel time series or pressure distributions. Even within optical sensors, variations in elastomer stiffness and lighting geometry alter appearance dramatically, not to mention manufacturing tolerances across individual units. These discrepancies make direct data reuse extremely challenging.

### The Shift in Tactile Representation Learning
Early studies explored self-supervised pre-training on single sensors or limited datasets (e.g., Sparsh), as well as sensor-specific encoders combined with a shared trunk (e.g., T3). Later methods like HTT and TactX attempted cross-sensor alignment by collecting paired observations under identical contact conditions. More recently, approaches like AnyTouch 2 have integrated 3-axis force prediction, while UniForce enforces static equilibrium constraints.

However, these works remain limited in sensor diversity and scale. They lack both strong few-shot transferability to unseen hardware and a unified representation directly grounded in full, measured 6D forces and torques. This paper sets itself apart by using an automated platform to collect massive real-world paired wrench data as a shared physical anchor.

### Application to Robotic Manipulation
Tactile feedback shines in tasks with occlusions and hand-level uncertainty. Recent efforts such as T-Rex, TaF-VLA, and NeoForce integrate tactile features directly into action policies. In this work, the shared tactile encoder pre-trained on diverse sensors is kept frozen and plugged into TaF-Policy, allowing a direct evaluation of representation generality and downstream transfer.

sections.heading: Over 100 million frames: an automated multi-axis rig for tactile-wrench collection
sections.summary: The authors built a dedicated test rig that simultaneously presses 24 tactile sensors against a 6-axis force/torque sensor. Across 1,445 sensor-probe combinations covering pressing, sliding, rotation, and rolling, they gathered over 100 million synchronized frames.
sections.details:
To achieve physics-grounded learning, one needs vast amounts of high-quality data where tactile observations and 6D wrenches are perfectly synchronized. Some earlier studies attempted to gather data by repeating the same trajectory separately on tactile and force sensors, but this inevitably introduces spatial and contact misalignments.

To solve this, the authors designed and built a custom test rig capable of contacting both sensors simultaneously while automatically generating diverse contact patterns.

- **Degrees of Freedom & Actuation**: Dynamixel actuators control yaw rotation (about the Z axis) and pressing torque along the Z axis. In addition, the probe fixture allows rotation around the X and Y axes, enabling arbitrary contact angles.
- **Motion Diversity**: Beyond simple linear pressing, the rig executes sliding, twisting/rotation, and rolling—covering the full spectrum of contact motions frequently encountered in manipulation.
- **Broad Variety**: By pairing 24 sensors (optical, magnetic, pressure, and piezoresistive) with over 200 swappable probe shapes, they collected data across 1,445 unique sensor-probe configurations.

A high-precision ATI Axia80-ZC22 sensor was used for ground-truth 6D wrench measurements, with bias calibration performed before each run. The resulting dataset contains 101,298,854 frames (30,503 episodes), recording force norms up to 90.81 N and torques up to 1.67 N·m. This unprecedented scale and variety form the bedrock of the foundation model.

captions.F3: Exploded and assembled views of the synchronized data collection platform. Combining Dynamixel servomotors, a rotary table, and a linear guide, it autonomously reproduces diverse contact motions (pressing, sliding, twisting, rolling) across X/Y/Z rotations and Z translation.

sections.heading: Align inputs via adapters, ground minds via wrenches: the TaF-Foundation architecture
sections.summary: Sensor-specific adapters project disparate inputs into 768-dimensional tokens, which are aggregated by a shared Transformer and a physical query. Wrench reconstruction and EMA embedding alignment then ground these features in physical contact mechanics.
sections.details:
### Unified Input Tokenization
Heterogeneous tactile inputs are first projected into sequences of shared 768-dimensional tokens:
1. **Image Inputs (Optical)**: The current tactile image and an uncompressed reference image are concatenated along the channel dimension (6 channels), divided into patches, and adapted via a sensor-specific residual MLP.
2. **Vector Inputs (Magnetic & Pressure Channels)**: Dynamic ranges are compressed using an $\operatorname{asinh}$ transform, then expanded into 32 tokens by a sensor-specific MLP.
3. **Pressure Matrices**: A 3-layer convolutional front-end produces feature maps that are flattened into tokens.
All tokens pass through sensor-family-specific projections, are prepended with a learnable sensor ID token, and are fed into the shared Transformer.

### Shared Encoder and Physical Query
After processing through 12 Transformer blocks initialized from DINOv2 ViT-B/14, a learnable physical query $\mathbf{q}$ aggregates contact mechanics across the entire sequence via cross-attention (QueryPool), producing a continuous 768-dimensional tactile representation $\mathbf{z}_i$.

### Wrench-Grounded Objectives
To anchor $\mathbf{z}_i$ in the physical world, the model incorporates a wrench encoder $g_\phi$ and a shared decoder $d_\psi$, optimizing a combination of three loss terms:
- **Wrench Reconstruction Loss**: Normalized ground-truth wrenches $\bar{\mathbf{w}}_i$ are mapped to a latent variable $\mathbf{u}_i$ by the wrench encoder and reconstructed by the decoder, training the wrench branch itself.
- **Tactile Wrench Prediction Loss**: Tactile representation $\mathbf{z}_i$ is passed into the decoder to predict the measured wrench. The decoder is frozen via stop-gradient so gradients flow exclusively into the tactile encoder.
- **Embedding Alignment Loss**: Minimizes the mean squared error between the tactile representation $\mathbf{z}_i$ and the target $\bar{\mathbf{u}}_i$ produced by an exponential moving average (EMA) copy of the wrench encoder.

### Downstream Policy Integration (TaF-Policy)
For robotic manipulation, the authors built TaF-Policy based on Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). Tactile features $\mathbf{z}$ from the left and right fingers are linearly projected into tactile tokens and concatenated with vision tokens (head and wrist cameras) and robot joint states to predict action chunks. During policy training, the pre-trained tactile encoder remains entirely frozen, and no wrench sensor is required at test time.

sections.heading: From force estimation to real-robot manipulation: validating strong generalization
sections.summary: The model substantially cuts force and torque estimation errors across 21 known sensors and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13 points. It also outperforms baselines in few-shot adaptation to 3 unseen sensors and in real-world robotic manipulation.
sections.details:
### Benchmark Evaluation: Representation Quality
Using 21 known sensors with the encoder frozen, linear evaluation heads were trained to assess representation quality (Table 2):
- **Single-Frame Wrench Estimation**: Achieved a force RMSE of 2.321 N and torque RMSE of 0.0657 N·m, cutting errors by 17.1% and 15.2%, respectively, compared to the strongest baselines (such as DINOv2 and AnyTouch 2).
- **Temporal Wrench Estimation**: Incorporating temporal history further boosted accuracy, reaching a force RMSE of 1.237 N (14.0% reduction) and a torque RMSE of 0.0322 N·m (6.1% reduction).
- **Cross-Sensor Retrieval**: Among 20 candidate observations from different sensors, the model retrieves the sample closest in true 6D wrench space using only distance in tactile feature space. TaF-Foundation achieved a top-1 accuracy (R@1) of 34.38%, outperforming the best baseline (21.27%) by 13.11 percentage points.

### Few-Shot Adaptation to Unseen Sensors
For three unseen sensors held out from pre-training (two optical, one magnetic), the backbone was kept frozen while only the input module and prediction head were adapted using small subsets of data (5% to 100%) (Fig. 5). The proposed method achieved the best hierarchical aggregate score of 0.4468, substantially outperforming existing models, particularly in data-rich regimes.

### Ablation Studies
Removing the alignment loss or relying strictly on direct wrench regression led to noticeable drops in performance. Crucially, removing the sensor-specific MLP adapters caused single-frame force RMSE to degrade from 2.415 N to 3.291 N and dropped retrieval R@1 to 25.90%, underscoring the necessity of adapters to absorb hardware calibration differences.

### Robotic Manipulation (Simulation & Real World)
- **UniVTAC Simulation**: Across three tasks (can lifting, key pull-out, and bottle shelving), the model achieved an average success rate of 51.33%, surpassing baselines including the official UniVTAC policy (best at 47.33%).
- **Real-World Experiments (Franka)**: Tested on four tasks: bottle lifting, power bank pulling, key insertion, and board wiping with a magnetic tactile sensor (Fig. 6). The strongest baseline evaluated on all four tasks achieved an average success rate of 23.75%, whereas TaF-Policy reached 46.25%—nearly double. On the three shared tasks, it led 40.0% vs. 18.3%.
The authors observe that real-world improvements were even more pronounced than in simulation. While simulated tactile images primarily capture contact geometry, real tactile images contain complex, force-induced deformations that wrench-grounded representations capture exceptionally well.

sections.heading: Conclusions and open challenges: toward hardware-agnostic tactile AI
sections.summary: By pairing over 100 million frames with wrench-grounded representation learning, this work establishes a robust tactile foundation model across heterogeneous sensors. Reducing label reliance for unseen sensors and achieving finer closed-loop control remain key next steps.
sections.details:
This paper introduced TaF-Foundation, grounding diverse tactile sensors into a single shared representation space by adopting 6D wrenches—fundamental quantities of Newtonian mechanics—as a universal anchor. Its effectiveness is demonstrated across a 100M+ frame dataset, representation benchmarks, adaptation to unseen hardware, and physical robotic contact manipulation.

Nevertheless, the authors highlight several practical limitations:
- **Label Dependency for Unseen Sensors**: Adapting to a brand-new sensor currently requires a small set of paired, wrench-labeled data to train the sensor-specific input module. Future work should explore frameworks capable of zero-shot transfer using unlabelled data alone.
- **Failures in Ultra-High-Precision Tasks**: In real-world manipulation, failures still occurred during sub-millimeter angular alignments (such as tight key insertion) or when handling slight slip-induced instability during bottle lifting. Developing higher-frequency tactile feedback loops will be essential to tackle dynamic slip detection and ultra-fine control.

takeaways: Tactile sensor heterogeneity (optical, magnetic, piezo, etc.) can be bridged by anchoring representations to physical 6D wrenches (forces and torques) rather than matching raw observations directly.
Large-scale synchronized data (100M+ frames across 24 sensors) paired with EMA embedding alignment yields significantly more generalizable features than direct regression alone.
Physics-grounded tactile representations provide massive performance gains—nearly doubling success rates—on physical robots, even more so than in simulation.
A frozen tactile encoder can transfer efficiently to unseen hardware simply by training lightweight, sensor-specific input adapters.
limitations: Adapting to unseen tactile sensors still requires a small amount of paired, wrench-labeled data and additional training of sensor-specific input adapters.
Tasks demanding sub-millimeter geometric alignment, such as inserting a key into a tight keyhole, can still fail.
Integrating representations into higher-frequency dynamic feedback loops (e.g., instant slip detection while lifting objects) remains an open challenge.
